title: Government & Defense Supply Chain RFID — MIL-STD-129R, MIL-STD-130N IUID, UID Compliance & Weapon Tracking
summary: DoD, federal-agency and prime-contractor supply chains serialize every controlled item and shipping container with RFID to satisfy MIL-STD-129R passive RFID marking of unit loads, MIL-STD-130N Item Unique Identification (IUID / UID) of serialized items ≥ $5,000, DFARS 252.211-7006 RFID data requirements, and weapon-system accountability (armory tracking, ammunition accountability, FOB weapon issue/return). Proud Tek supplies DoD Tier-2 passive UHF RFID tags (Impinj M730 / M750, NXP UCODE 9 on ceramic / PPS substrate), NTAG424 DNA authenticated part nameplates, weapon-stock UHF tags and the pre-encoded EPC services that comply with DoD Wide Area Workflow (WAWF) iRFID submissions.

Weapon-system accountability ready — weapon-stock UHF tags and armory-portal workflow supporting FOB, armory and ammunition-accountability programs across all services.

sections.title: Challenges government and defense supply chains face without RFID
bullets: DoD shipment rejection without MIL-STD-129R passive UHF RFID — since 2005 the DoD has mandated passive UHF RFID marking on palletized unit loads shipped to designated DoD consignees (DFARS 252.211-7006); shipments arriving without compliant tags are rejected at the receiving dock and the prime-contractor loses both that shipment and future-award points.

IUID non-compliance as DCMA audit finding — MIL-STD-130N requires a machine-readable unique identifier on every DoD-controlled item ≥ $5,000 (and on designated lower-value mission-critical items); contractors missing IUID marking get cited in DCMA audits, which cascades into CPARS performance ratings and source-selection penalties.

Armory and weapon-accountability paper logs — handwritten weapon-issue logs at arms-room and FOB armory produce chronic mis-counts that trigger investigation and recovery procedures; RFID-tagged weapons and portal readers reduce weapon-accountability miscounts from 0.3-1.1% per issue event to under 0.01%.

Ammunition accountability across range operations — ammo-can tracking across training ranges, FOB storage and mission issue is a chronic accountability burden; unit-level RFID on ammo cans and pallets eliminates the reconciliation overhead.

Counterfeit parts ingress from the defense aftermarket — counterfeit microelectronics and fasteners in the defense supply chain have been a documented problem since the 2012 Senate Armed Services investigation; cryptographic NTAG424 DNA authentication on approved-supplier part nameplates blocks counterfeit ingress at incoming inspection.

Chain of custody for classified-media disposal — NIST SP 800-88 plus DoDM 5200.01 Vol 3 require documented chain of custody for classified media destruction; tamper-evident NFC tags provide cryptographic SUN-code evidence that holds up in security review.

faq.question: Is RFID mandatory for DoD shipments?
faq.answer: Yes — DFARS 252.211-7006 requires passive UHF RFID on palletized unit loads shipped to designated DoD consignees, per MIL-STD-129R. The clause flows down to prime contractors and subcontractors. Shipments arriving without compliant tags are rejected at receiving and can trigger CPARS performance findings against the contractor.

faq.question: What is IUID / UID and is it separate from MIL-STD-129R?
faq.answer: Yes — they are separate but complementary. IUID (Item Unique Identification, MIL-STD-130N) applies to individual controlled items (not shipments) valued ≥ $5,000 or designated mission-critical. MIL-STD-129R applies to shipment unit loads. An aircraft LRU typically carries an IUID plate per MIL-STD-130N AND ships on a pallet with MIL-STD-129R RFID marking — both requirements apply simultaneously.

faq.question: Do you support Berry Amendment and TAA compliance?
faq.answer: Yes. Proud Tek provides country-of-origin documentation for every material in the tag/label construction and can route production to TAA-compliant designated-country factories when the contract DFARS 252.225-7001 / 7012 / 7020 require. Contact us with your contract clause list and we'll confirm qualification.

faq.question: How does RFID weapon tracking work in an armory?
faq.answer: Each weapon (M4, M9, crew-served, optics, NVG) is tagged with a slim on-metal UHF tag. The armory doorway has a fixed UHF portal reader. Issue and return are captured automatically by the portal; the armorer confirms the reading against the issue log before the weapon leaves the building. End-of-shift accountability sweep completes in under 60 seconds versus 20-40 minutes manual counting. Tags survive normal weapon use and cleaning cycles.

faq.question: Can Proud Tek support WAWF iRFID submission?
faq.answer: Yes — Proud Tek pre-encodes EPC headers and serial ranges to match your DoD CAGE code and GS1 Company Prefix so the tags arrive WAWF-ready. The encoded EPC data flows directly into the WAWF Advance Shipment Notice (ASN) without additional re-encoding equipment on the prime contractor's dock.
